root.note: Back to an Indo-European word for water, reconstructed as *h₂ekʷeh₂. It is not the source of English water.

history: Agua is a word Spanish simply inherited: Latin aqua became agua with hardly a change. The Latin word goes back to an Indo-European word for water, but not every related language used it. Another old root, *wed-, gave English water, German Wasser and Greek hýdōr. That is why Spanish has two sets of water words: acuario and acuarela from Latin, hídrico and hidráulico from Greek. Agua is also a famous grammar trap. It is feminine, but you say el agua, because feminine nouns beginning with a stressed a- take el in the singular. Everything else stays feminine: el agua fría, las aguas.
historyEinfach: Agua comes from Latin aqua. It changed very little. English water is not related to it: water comes from a different old word. Be careful with the grammar. Agua is a feminine word, but we say el agua. Why? It begins with a stressed a. Other words stay feminine: el agua fría, las aguas.

elsewhere.text: It takes some imagination, but eau is the same Latin word as agua, worn down by centuries of French sound changes.
Italian acqua stays closest to the Latin.
Portuguese água is the same word, but its article is a água: Spanish el agua is a surprise for Portuguese speakers.
English water and agua mean the same thing but come from two separate old roots.
German Wasser belongs with English water, not with agua.
